hero.title: Your master password never leaves your browser
hero.subtitle: This server stores your data but cannot read it. That is not a promise you have to trust: it follows from how the keys are built. On this page you can check it yourself, right here, with the app's real cryptography.

keys.title: How the keys are born
keys.description: Everything starts with your master password and ends in two different things: one that travels to the server and decrypts nothing, and one that never leaves your device.
keys.note: The server receives the authHash and hashes it again with bcrypt. Even if the whole database were stolen, there is nothing there to open a vault with: the wrapKey, which wraps the vault key, stays on this side.

demo.title: See it for yourself
demo.description: Type a throwaway master password and something to store. Everything below is computed in your browser with the very same functions the app uses: none of it is sent anywhere.
demo.kdfTime: Argon2id took {{ms}} ms on your device. An attacker guessing your master password pays that cost on EVERY attempt.
demo.travels: This is the only thing that travels to the server
demo.travelsNote: The authHash cannot be turned back into your password and decrypts nothing. The server also re-hashes it with bcrypt before storing it.
demo.staysNote: The wrapKey wraps the vault key. If it never leaves here, the server cannot unwrap it.
demo.stored: This is what the database stores
demo.storedNote: That is how your data looks on the server: the whole row, as-is. Without the vault key it is noise.
demo.decrypted: And this is how your browser gets it back
demo.tamper: Flip one byte of the ciphertext
demo.tamperNote: AES-GCM is authenticated: if the server changes a single byte of your encrypted data, decryption does not return garbage, it fails. There is no silent way to alter what you stored.
demo.tamperError: Decryption rejected: the data was tampered with.

scenarios.title: What happens if…
scenarios.leakText: The attacker walks away with encrypted blobs and bcrypt hashes of authHashes. To open a vault they would have to guess the master password and pay for Argon2id with 64 MiB of memory on every attempt.
scenarios.liesText: A compromised server could delete items or hand you an older version. That is why your browser signs an encrypted inventory of what you stored: if something is missing, changed or rolled back, the app warns you when you open the vault.
scenarios.masterText: That is what the recovery key shown once at sign-up is for. It wraps the same vault key, so it opens your data and lets you set a new master password without losing anything.
scenarios.bothText: It is gone. Nobody can recover your vault, not you and not whoever runs the server. That sounds harsh, and it is exactly the proof that the rest is true: if a service door existed, it would exist for anyone who takes over the server.

limits.title: The limits, unvarnished
limits.intro: No system is bulletproof. These are the risks that remain, stated plainly:
limits.xssTitle: An XSS in the front-end would be serious
limits.xssText: While the vault is open, the key lives in browser memory. Malicious code running on the page could reach it. That is why the app ships a strict Content-Security-Policy with no external scripts, and why the vault locks itself on inactivity.
limits.hostTitle: Whoever serves the site serves the code
limits.hostText: In any web-based password manager, whoever controls the server could hand you modified JavaScript. That is the model's inherent limit. What you can do is read the code and compare what your browser downloads.
limits.masterTitle: A weak master password is still weak
limits.masterText: Argon2id makes each attempt expensive, but it does not fix a six-letter password. The strength of the whole vault starts with the one you choose.
limits.deviceTitle: Your device is part of the system
limits.deviceText: A machine with malware, a keylogger, or someone reading over your shoulder defeats any cryptography. Encryption protects data in transit and at rest on the server, not the screen you are looking at.

verify.title: You do not have to take my word
verify.text: Open your developer tools, Network tab, and sign up. You will see the authHash and encrypted blobs go out; you will not see your master password or the contents of a single item. It is the same check the demo above performs, but against real traffic.
